The Apostles' Creed
8th century (received form)
The ancient Western baptismal creed, which confesses that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead and affirms the resurrection of the body.
Standard text; URL not fetched during research.

Two days before the cross, Jesus sat on the Mount of Olives and looked across the valley at the temple. Four of His disciples had just admired its great stones. He told them that not one stone would be left on another. Then they asked Him three questions: when will this happen, what will be the sign of your coming, and what will mark the end of the age? His answer fills Matthew 24 and 25. This study walks through that answer verse by verse, as fulfilled-prophecy (preterist) interpreters read it. The fulfilled reading makes one main claim. Jesus was speaking to these men about events they would live to see. He said that 'this generation' would not pass away before all these things happened (Matthew 24:34). About forty years later, in AD 70, Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem and burned the temple. This reading holds that the false messiahs, wars, persecution, flight, siege and judgment of the discourse all belong to those forty years. It also reads the language of the sun darkening and the Son of Man coming on the clouds as Old Testament judgment language, not as a picture of the end of the physical world. Why does this matter? If the reading is right, Jesus kept His word to the very people He spoke to. The discourse then becomes a record of His faithfulness, not a timetable of fear. Believers are freed to stop reading the news for signs, and to give themselves to the work of His kingdom. You do not have to agree with every step to learn from it. Read the text slowly, ask the five simple questions, weigh the ancient historians, and see each verse alongside how other Christians read it. Then decide for yourself.

Where does this reading sit among Christians? It helps to separate two forms of it. Partial preterists hold that most of Matthew 24 was fulfilled in the Jewish War of AD 66-70. This includes the great tribulation and the judgment on the temple. But they still expect a future, bodily return of Christ, a general resurrection of the dead, and a final judgment. Writers such as Kenneth Gentry, R. C. Sproul and Keith Mathison hold this view. Many of them place the turn to the final coming at Matthew 24:36 or in Matthew 25:31-46. Full preterists (sometimes called 'covenant eschatology'; critics call it 'hyper-preterism') go further. They hold that the Second Coming, the resurrection and the judgment were also fulfilled in connection with AD 70. The reading presented in this study follows that fuller form, since it applies Matthew 25, including the judgment of the sheep and the goats, to the first century. This fuller form stands outside the historic creeds. The Apostles' Creed confesses that Christ 'will come to judge the living and the dead' and affirms 'the resurrection of the body'. The Nicene Creed says that He will come again in glory to judge, and that the church looks for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. Critics give several reasons for rejecting full preterism. First, the whole church in every age has confessed a future return and resurrection. Second, Paul teaches a bodily resurrection in which death itself, the last enemy, is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26, 15:54), and death is still with us. Third, the angels promised that Jesus would come back in the same way He went up (Acts 1:11). Fourth, Paul warned against Hymenaeus and Philetus, who said the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:17-18). Fifth, the Lord's Supper proclaims His death 'until He comes' (1 Corinthians 11:26), and the church has kept it ever since. Full preterists reply in turn. They say the creeds are valuable summaries but stand under Scripture, and that Scripture's time statements must decide the matter. They read the resurrection of 1 Corinthians 15 as the raising of God's people out of the realm of death at the close of the old covenant age, or as believers receiving new life at death. They note that 2 Timothy was written before AD 70, so Hymenaeus was wrong because he spoke too early, not because the resurrection was never near. They read Acts 1:11 as a promise that He would come in clouds, as He left in a cloud. And they hold that 'until He comes' fitted a church that lived before AD 70. Partial preterists agree with full preterists on much of Matthew 24 but side with the creeds on these points. Futurist, historicist and idealist readers see the discourse differently again. To compare all these views side by side, see the app's Olivet Discourse study.
Who is speaking, and to whom?

Jesus is speaking. Matthew 24:3 says only that 'the disciples' came to Him privately. Mark 13:3 names them: Peter, James, John and Andrew, two pairs of brothers. The fulfilled reading stresses that the word 'you' in the discourse first means these four men. Matthew, a former tax collector and one of the Twelve, later wrote it down for early believers, many of them Jewish.
What is the discourse about?

It begins with the temple. Jesus says it will be thrown down. The disciples then ask when this will be, what the sign of His coming will be, and what the end of the age will be. The answer covers deceivers, wars, persecution, the 'abomination of desolation', a great tribulation, the coming of the Son of Man, the fig tree lesson, and parables about readiness. The fulfilled reading takes 'the end of the age' as the end of the old covenant age centred on the temple, not the end of the world.
Where is Jesus, and where will these things happen?

He is sitting on the Mount of Olives, a ridge east of Jerusalem that looks across the Kidron Valley to the temple. The places named in the discourse are local: the holy place, Judea, its mountains, flat housetops and fields. Luke adds Jerusalem surrounded by armies. The fulfilled reading sees this local detail as a clue that the warnings concern Judea and Jerusalem in that century.
When did Jesus speak, and when would it happen?

He spoke in the last week before the cross, in the spring of about AD 30 or AD 33, depending on the chronology used. He set the time limit Himself: 'this generation' would not pass away until all these things took place. The Jewish revolt began in AD 66. Titus besieged Jerusalem in the spring and summer of AD 70, and the temple burned in late summer of that year, about forty years later.
Why did Jesus give this teaching?

To prepare His followers. He warned them not to be deceived by false messiahs, told them to endure, and gave them a clear signal to flee to the mountains. The fall of Jerusalem was one of the worst disasters in Jewish history, and the city and temple were the centre of Jewish life. Jesus wanted His people ready, faithful and alive. The parables of Matthew 25 add that they should be watchful, faithful with what He gave them, and kind to the least of His brothers.
Born in Jerusalem about AD 37 into a priestly family; died about AD 100, probably in Rome.

Josephus is the main eyewitness of the war. He commanded Jewish forces in Galilee, surrendered to Vespasian at Jotapata in AD 67, and later served Titus as an interpreter during the siege of Jerusalem. His Jewish War describes the false prophets, the factions, the famine, the burning of the temple (Jewish War 6.4.5-8) and the numbers of the dead and captured (Jewish War 6.9.3). The fulfilled reading relies on him more than on any other ancient writer. His Antiquities also mentions John the Baptist (18.5.2), James the brother of Jesus (20.9.1) and, in a disputed passage, Jesus Himself (18.3.3).

Josephus wrote under Roman patronage and wanted to flatter Vespasian and Titus. He blames the war on a few Jewish rebels and paints himself in a good light. Ancient writers often rounded or inflated large numbers, so his figures (such as 1,100,000 dead) are debated. He never mentions the Olivet Discourse, so links between his account and Jesus' words are drawn by interpreters.
Cornelius Tacitus
About AD 56 to about AD 120. A Roman senator who became consul in AD 97 and later governed the province of Asia.

Tacitus is an independent Roman witness. In Histories 5.1-13 he describes the Jews, the start of Titus' siege, and strange signs reported in the temple. In Histories 5.13 he says many Jews believed ancient priestly writings foretold that men from Judea would rule the world at that time. In Annals 15.44 he tells of Nero blaming the Christians for the fire of Rome in AD 64 and mentions 'Christus', executed under Pontius Pilate. He also records the earthquake that struck Laodicea in AD 60 (Annals 14.27).

Tacitus was not an eyewitness of the war, and he wrote about thirty years later. He openly despised Jews and Christians. His account of the siege breaks off near its start, so his description of the fall itself is lost.
Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus
About AD 69 to after AD 122. A scholar and imperial secretary under Trajan and Hadrian.

Suetonius supplies the background of the emperors who ruled during the New Testament period. In Vespasian 4.5 he says that an old and settled belief spread through the East that men from Judea would rule the world at that time, and that the Jews applied it to themselves and revolted. He also mentions Claudius expelling Jews from Rome (Claudius 25.4, compare Acts 18:2) and Nero punishing Christians (Nero 16.2).
Suetonius was not an eyewitness. He loved anecdotes and gossip, and he organised his lives by topic rather than by date. He gives few details of the Jewish War itself.
About AD 260 to about AD 339. Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine.

Eusebius is the first great historian of the church. He preserves the report that Jerusalem's Christians were warned to leave the city before the war and settled in Pella, east of the Jordan (Church History 3.5.3). He quotes Josephus at length on the siege and famine (3.5-3.8) and presents the fall of Jerusalem as judgment for the rejection of Christ. He also records Irenaeus' statement that John saw the Revelation near the end of Domitian's reign (3.18; 5.8), which is central to the debate on Revelation's date.

Eusebius wrote more than 250 years after the events. He often depended on earlier writers whose works are now lost, and he wrote with a clear theological purpose. Some scholars question the Pella tradition, though others defend its historical core.
The King arrives

Holy Week begins with Jesus riding into Jerusalem on a donkey's colt. Matthew says this fulfils Zechariah 9:9, the humble king coming to Zion. The crowds hail Him as the Son of David. The fulfilled reading notes that the King has come to His city. What follows is His final appeal to it, and then His verdict on it.
The temple cleansed

Jesus drives out those who buy and sell in the temple courts. He joins Isaiah 56:7 (a house of prayer) with Jeremiah 7:11 (a den of robbers). In Jeremiah 7 that charge came just before the first temple was destroyed. Many interpreters see a warning here: the second temple was heading for the same end.
The fruitless fig tree

Jesus finds leaves but no fruit on a fig tree, and it withers. Many interpreters read this as an acted parable. In the prophets the fig tree can picture Israel (Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10). A nation full of religious show but without fruit faces judgment. Jesus adds that faith could say to 'this mountain' be thrown into the sea, which some take as a hint at the temple mount. Others read the sign more generally, as a lesson about empty religion that hides sin instead of removing it.
The tenants and the son

A landowner sends servants to collect fruit from his vineyard. The tenants beat and kill them, and at last kill his son. In the story, God is the owner, the leaders of Israel are the tenants, the prophets are the servants, and Jesus is the son. Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22, the rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone. He then says the kingdom will be taken from them and given to a people who produce its fruit (Matthew 21:43). The leaders understood that He was speaking about them.
The wedding feast and the burned city

A king prepares a wedding feast for his son. Those invited refuse, and some kill his servants. The king sends his armies, destroys those murderers and burns their city (Matthew 22:7). Then the invitation goes out to everyone in the streets. The fulfilled reading sees the burned city as Jerusalem in AD 70, and the new guests as the Gentiles who came into the church.
Questions in the temple

Pharisees, Herodians, Sadducees and a lawyer each try to trap Jesus: on taxes to Caesar, on the resurrection, and on the greatest commandment. He answers each one, then asks how the Messiah can be both David's son and David's Lord (Psalm 110:1). After that, no one dares to question Him. The leaders have rejected Him, and the stage is set for His judgment speech.
The woes and 'this generation'

Jesus pronounces a series of woes on the scribes and Pharisees, in the style of the prophets (Isaiah 5:8-23; Habakkuk 2:6-19). Some manuscripts count eight woes, most modern texts seven. He tells them to fill up the measure of their fathers, who killed the prophets. All the righteous blood shed on the earth, from Abel to Zechariah, will come on them. Then He says that all these things will come upon this generation (Matthew 23:36). The fulfilled reading treats this as the key to chapter 24. The same people, and the same time limit, are in view.
Your house is left desolate

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets. He longed to gather its children as a hen gathers her chicks, but they would not come. Then He says, 'Your house is left to you desolate.' The 'house' is most likely the temple. In the very next verse, Jesus leaves the temple and the disciples point out its buildings (Matthew 24:1). The chapter break hides how closely these scenes belong together.
The setting: the King and His city

Before Matthew 24, read Matthew 21-23. Jesus enters Jerusalem as king, cleanses the temple, curses a fruitless fig tree, and tells parables of rejected servants and a burned city. He ends with woes on the leaders, the promise that all these things will come on 'this generation', and the words 'your house is left to you desolate'. The discourse grows out of this setting.
Not one stone on another

Jesus leaves the temple. The disciples point out its great buildings. He says every stone will be thrown down. In AD 70 Titus' army burned the temple and later levelled the city. The Arch of Titus in Rome still shows the temple lampstand carried in triumph.
The beginning of birth pains

The disciples ask when, what sign, and what end. Jesus warns of false messiahs, wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution, betrayal and false prophets. But the end is not yet. First the gospel must be preached in the whole inhabited world. The fulfilled reading finds each of these in Acts, the letters and Josephus between AD 30 and 70.
The abomination and the great tribulation

When they see the abomination of desolation, those in Judea must flee at once. Jesus describes a distress worse than any before or after, days cut short for the elect, and false christs with signs. The fulfilled reading links this to Jerusalem surrounded by armies (Luke 21:20), the flight to Pella, and the siege of AD 70.
The Son of Man coming on the clouds

Sun and moon darken, stars fall, and the tribes mourn as they see the Son of Man coming on the clouds. The fulfilled reading hears the language of the prophets, who used such pictures for the fall of nations, and reads it as Christ's coming in judgment on Jerusalem and the gathering of His people through the gospel.
This generation will not pass away

Learn from the fig tree: when you see these things, He is near, at the doors. This generation will not pass away until all these things happen. Heaven and earth will pass away, but His words will not. The fulfilled reading holds that this verse sets the time for everything before it.
No one knows the day or the hour

The exact day and hour are known only to the Father. As in Noah's day, people will carry on with life until judgment sweeps them away. One will be taken and one left. So keep watch, like a householder expecting a thief. The fulfilled reading sees the generation as fixed but the day unknown, and the one 'taken' as taken in judgment.

A faithful servant feeds the household until his master comes. A wicked servant says 'my master is delayed', beats his fellow servants and lives with drunkards. The master comes unexpectedly and punishes him with the hypocrites. The fulfilled reading sees a warning to leaders in that generation.
Three parables of the end of the age

Ten virgins wait for the bridegroom. Servants are given talents to trade with until their master returns. The Son of Man sits on His throne and divides the sheep from the goats by how they treated the least of His brothers. The fulfilled reading, in its full form, applies all three to the coming of Christ in that generation.
The disciples admire the Temple
shew him the buildings of the temple

Jesus has just pronounced woes on the leaders and said their house is left desolate (Matthew 23:38). Now He walks out of the Temple. The disciples point to its great buildings, as if to ask how such a place could ever fall. In the fulfilled reading, His leaving the Temple is a sign that God's presence is departing from it.

Herod the Great began rebuilding the Temple in about 20/19 BC. Work on the wider complex went on for decades and was only finished in about AD 63-64, under the governor Albinus. So the great buildings were completed only a few years before the Romans destroyed them in AD 70.
Josephus says Herod began the rebuilding in the eighteenth year of his reign.
Josephus reports that the work was finished under Albinus, and about 18,000 workers lost their jobs.
Josephus describes huge white stones and a front covered with gold that shone like the sun.
Most readers of every view agree that this verse describes Herod's Temple. Futurist readers usually see the setting as the start of a discourse that later moves to a distant end-time.
The fulfilled reader agrees on the setting and adds that nothing in the scene suggests a change of subject. The disciples ask about the building in front of them.
There shall not be left here one stone upon another

Jesus answers the disciples' admiration with a plain prediction. The whole Temple complex they are looking at will be torn down. The word 'here' points to the buildings in front of them. The fulfilled reading takes this as the anchor of the whole discourse: everything that follows answers when and how this would happen.

In AD 70 the Roman army under Titus captured Jerusalem. The Temple burned on the ninth or tenth of the month Av, about late August AD 70. Titus then ordered the city and Temple to be razed. The Arch of Titus in Rome, built after his death in AD 81, shows soldiers carrying away the Temple's lampstand.
Josephus says the Temple burned on the tenth of the month Lous (Av), the same day the first Temple had burned.
Josephus says Titus ordered the city and Temple demolished. Only three towers and part of the western city wall were left standing.
The relief on the arch shows Roman soldiers carrying the menorah and other Temple objects in triumph.
Futurist readers agree that this verse was fulfilled in AD 70. Some point to the large stones still standing in the Western Wall and say the prophecy was not completed in every detail.

The fulfilled reader replies that the Western Wall is part of the retaining wall of the Temple platform, not the Temple buildings the disciples showed Jesus. Those buildings were completely destroyed.
One question about the Temple
what shall be the sign of thy coming

On the Mount of Olives, four disciples ask privately: when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of His coming and of the end of the age? The fulfilled reading treats this as one question with three parts, all tied to the Temple's fall. 'The end of the age' means the end of the Old Covenant age with its Temple and sacrifices, not the end of the planet.

The discourse was spoken in the last week of Jesus' ministry, about AD 30 or 33. Within about forty years the Temple was destroyed in AD 70. With it, the sacrifices of the Mosaic system came to an end.
Josephus records that the daily sacrifice in the Temple stopped during the siege of AD 70 for lack of men to offer it.
aion (αἰών)
age, a span of time

The disciples ask about the 'end of the age' (synteleia tou aionos), not the end of the world (kosmos). The fulfilled reading sees the age as the Old Covenant era. Hebrews 9:26 says Christ appeared 'at the end of the ages', in the first century.
Futurist readers often see the question as two or three separate questions. They hold that Jesus answers the Temple question in part and then speaks about a coming at the end of world history.
The fulfilled reader notes that Mark and Luke record only a question about 'these things'. This suggests the disciples expected the coming and the end of the age to happen with the Temple's fall.
Do not be deceived
Take heed that no man deceive you

Jesus' first word is a warning about deception. In the fulfilled reading, 'you' means the disciples sitting with Him. Mark 13:3 names them: Peter, James, John and Andrew. The warning prepared them for a real danger in their own lifetime. The apostles later passed the same warning on to the early churches.

In the years before AD 70, many teachers and leaders drew people away with false hopes. Paul warned the churches not to be shaken by false reports (2 Thessalonians 2:2-3). Some interpreters in this reading identify Paul's 'man of lawlessness' with a figure of the Jewish War, such as Titus or the Zealot leaders. Others in the same reading disagree.
Josephus describes deceivers who claimed divine inspiration and led crowds astray under the governor Felix.
Futurist readers see the 'you' as the disciples standing for all believers, especially those alive at the end of history.
The fulfilled reader agrees the lesson applies to every Christian. But the first meaning belongs to the people Jesus addressed, who would see these things.
Many will claim to be the Christ
many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ

Jesus warns that many will come using His name or claiming the role of Messiah. The fulfilled reading points to the many impostors and would-be deliverers who appeared in Judea between Jesus' death and AD 70. The New Testament itself names some of them.

About AD 44-46 Theudas led a crowd to the Jordan, promising the river would part. Under Felix, in the mid-50s, an Egyptian prophet gathered followers on the Mount of Olives. He promised that Jerusalem's walls would fall at his command. Roman troops killed or scattered both groups.
Josephus says Theudas claimed to be a prophet and promised to divide the Jordan. The governor Fadus sent cavalry, and Theudas was beheaded.
Josephus says an Egyptian false prophet led a crowd to the Mount of Olives. Felix attacked and most were killed or captured.
A Roman officer asks Paul if he is the Egyptian who led 4,000 'assassins' into the wilderness.
Futurist readers expect a great increase of false messiahs before Christ's return, and many see a final Antichrist in view.
The fulfilled reader points out that John already said 'many antichrists have come' and that it was 'the last hour' (1 John 2:18). The warning was being fulfilled in the apostles' own day.
ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars

Jesus tells the disciples not to panic when they hear of wars, because 'the end is not yet'. In the fulfilled reading, 'the end' is the end of the age asked about in verse 3: the fall of the Temple. Wars and threats of war would come first, but they were not the final sign.

Jesus spoke during the Roman peace (Pax Romana). In AD 40 Caligula ordered his statue placed in the Temple, and war nearly broke out. In AD 66 the Jewish revolt began. In AD 68-69, after Nero's death, Rome itself fell into civil war, with four emperors in one year.
Josephus describes Caligula's order to set up his statue in the Temple and the alarm it caused in Judea.
Tacitus describes the period as full of disasters, savage battles and civil strife, with four emperors killed.
Futurist readers see an increase of wars across the world as a general sign of the age, growing stronger before Christ returns.
The fulfilled reader replies that Jesus spoke to people who would 'hear' of these wars. Within forty years the peaceful empire was shaken by revolt and civil war, just as He said.
Famines, pestilences and earthquakes
famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, in divers places

Jesus foretells conflict between nations and kingdoms, along with famines, diseases and earthquakes in various places. The fulfilled reading looks for these within the Roman world before AD 70. It finds them recorded both in Acts and in Roman and Jewish historians.

A severe famine struck Judea under Claudius, about AD 46-48, as Agabus had predicted (Acts 11:28). Earthquakes shook the Roman province of Asia and Italy: Laodicea in AD 60 and Pompeii in Campania in AD 62. A plague in Rome in AD 65 killed many thousands. In AD 66, Jews and Syrians fought in many cities.
Josephus says Queen Helena of Adiabene bought grain from Egypt for Jerusalem during a great famine.
Tacitus records that Laodicea was destroyed by an earthquake in AD 60 and rebuilt from its own resources.
Tacitus describes a deadly plague in Rome in AD 65.
Futurist readers expect these troubles to grow in number and strength in the last days before Christ's return.
The fulfilled reader notes that such events have happened in every age. Jesus gave them to His hearers as signs they would see within their own lifetime.
All these are the beginning of sorrows

Jesus calls these troubles the beginning of birth pains. Birth pains are painful, but they lead to new life. In the fulfilled reading, the old covenant order was passing away while the new covenant community was being born. The years from the cross to AD 70 were a time of transition.

The forty years from about AD 30 to AD 70 saw the church grow while Jerusalem moved toward war. The pains grew stronger until the Temple fell. After that, the church stood clearly apart from the old Temple system.
odin (ὠδίν)
birth pain, labour pain

The word describes the pains of a woman in labour. The prophets used it for a time of distress that ends in a new beginning (Isaiah 66:7-8). It suggests sharp pains that come closer together, followed by a birth.
Futurist readers often link the birth pains to a final period of trouble before the Messiah's kingdom. Some connect them to a future seven-year tribulation.
The fulfilled reader replies that the birth was near at hand. The new covenant people were coming to birth in the first century, and the old covenant was 'ready to vanish away' (Hebrews 8:13).
ye shall be hated of all nations

Jesus warns the disciples that they will be handed over, afflicted and killed, and hated by all nations for His name. The fulfilled reading sees this fulfilled in the persecutions recorded in Acts and in Roman history. These came first from Jerusalem's leaders and later from Rome.

Stephen was stoned in Jerusalem, perhaps about AD 34. James son of Zebedee was killed by Herod Agrippa I in about AD 44. James the brother of Jesus was stoned in Jerusalem in AD 62. In AD 64 Nero blamed the Christians for the great fire of Rome.
Josephus says the high priest Ananus had James, 'the brother of Jesus who was called Christ', and others stoned.
Tacitus says the Christians were hated for their supposed crimes and were punished by Nero.
Eusebius records the death of James the Just in Jerusalem.
Futurist readers often see a final, worldwide persecution of believers in the end times, in addition to past persecutions.
